title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
An AI music generation system was deployed commercially while its training data allegedly included copyrighted recordings it had no license to use. The core failure is straightforward: the system was trained on material belonging to third parties without their authorization, and it reached public deployment before any licensing agreements were in place. That gap between training-data acquisition and legal clearance is where the problem arose, not in the model's outputs or a failure of real-time filtering.

The incident involves multiple separate legal actions. Universal Music Group settled its claims and moved to a licensing arrangement requiring only authorized music in future training. Warner Music Group reached a similar resolution. Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit, alleging approximately 30,000 recordings were copied for training purposes, and a court declined to allow those recordings to be added to an earlier Sony case, leading Sony to file a new action. Independent artists also pursued a copyright class action, which a court declined to dismiss. What is not established is any finding of liability, since lawsuits are allegations and settlements do not constitute admissions.

Catching this class of failure requires rights clearance before training begins, not after a product launches. The settlements that followed show such clearance is achievable, but it was not the starting condition. The shift Udio agreed to, using only licensed material for future training, illustrates what the compliant version of this deployment would have looked like from the outset.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve the dispute. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, including The Temptations' hit "My Girl." Under the settlement, Udio has agreed to launch a new platform next year that will only use authorized and licensed music for training its AI, allowing users to create original songs from text prompts while ensuring artists and songwriters receive compensation.

The settlement marks Udio's first major licensing agreement with a large music label and represents a shift toward collaboration between the music industry and AI technology companies. Udio's CEO expressed enthusiasm about working with UMG to develop tools that empower both artists and fans. The financial terms of the settlement were not disclosed. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI on Thursday to create music creation tools for artists and producers.
